Data commands are **local-first**: they read and write a SQLite store with no server required, and switch to a remote MCP server with `--backend mcp`. Launch it with: ```bash python -m cli --version # print the Agentic ODI version python -m cli --help # show available options and commands python -m cli # start interactive chat in a terminal (help when piped) ``` A console script is also installed, so `agentic-odi --version` works the same way. **Global options:** | Option | Environment variable | Default | Meaning | |---|---|---|---| | `--backend local\|mcp` | `AGENTIC_ODI_BACKEND` | `local` | Run in-process against SQLite, or call a remote MCP server. | | `--db PATH` | `AGENTIC_ODI_DB` | `~/.agentic-odi/odi.db` | Store path for the `local` backend. | | `--mcp-url URL` | `AGENTIC_ODI_MCP_URL` | `http://localhost:8000/mcp` | Server URL for the `mcp` backend. | Data commands print readable tables and blocks by default; add `--json` for machine-readable output. Diagnostics go to stderr and failures exit non-zero (`0` success, `1` error, `2` usage error). ### 💬 Interactive Chat `agentic-odi chat` (or simply `agentic-odi` in a terminal) starts a conversational session against the MCP server and an OpenAI-compatible LLM. Responses stream to the terminal, and the assistant can call the ODI MCP tools as it talks. ```bash agentic-odi chat agentic-odi chat --model local-tools-model --mcp-url http://localhost:8000/mcp ``` Before starting, run the MCP server (`python -m mcp_server`) and point the chat at an OpenAI-compatible model endpoint. The chat reads the same environment variables as the Living Studio: | Variable | Default | CLI flag | |---|---|---| | `AGENTIC_ODI_BASE_URL` | `http://localhost:8001/v1` | `--base-url` | | `AGENTIC_ODI_MODEL` | `local-tools-model` | `--model` | | `AGENTIC_ODI_API_KEY` | `local` | `--api-key` | | `AGENTIC_ODI_MCP_URL` | `http://localhost:8000/mcp` | `--mcp-url` | Inside the session, `/help` lists the commands, `/tools` lists the MCP tools the assistant can call, `/clear` resets the conversation, and `/exit` (or `/quit`) ends the session. > [!NOTE] > Chat is the only CLI mode that needs an LLM endpoint. The `customer-outcomes` and `connectors` commands keep working without one. ### 🎯 Manage Customer Outcomes Customer Outcomes link customer value to business value. The `local` backend writes to the shared SQLite store with no server required; add `--backend mcp` to route through a running MCP server (`python -m mcp_server`). The group is also available under its historical name `outcomes`. ```bash # Add a Customer Outcome agentic-odi customer-outcomes add --job-id --direction minimize --unit "time" --object "to resolve setup errors" --statement "Minimize the time to resolve environment setup errors when onboarding" --importance 8.8 --satisfaction 3.2 --category cost_reduction --business-statement "Saves engineering hours and reduces early churn" # List outcomes (optionally filtered, or as JSON) agentic-odi customer-outcomes list agentic-odi customer-outcomes list --job-id agentic-odi customer-outcomes list --json # Get, update, delete agentic-odi customer-outcomes get agentic-odi customer-outcomes update --importance 9.0 agentic-odi customer-outcomes delete --yes # Compute ODI Opportunity Score (top-level, also under the group) agentic-odi score 8 2 agentic-odi outcomes score 8 2 ``` Set `AGENTIC_ODI_MCP_URL` (or `--mcp-url`) to point to a non-default server when using `--backend mcp`. ### 🔌 External Connectors (MCP Ingest) Connectors are named integrations stored in `.agentic-odi/connectors.json` (or a path you pass with `--config` / `AGENTIC_ODI_CONNECTORS_FILE`). The first kind is `mcp`: Agentic ODI acts as an MCP **client** and pulls catalog, resources, and optional tool results from an external MCP **server**. The fastest way to connect is a preset. `connectors catalog` lists every built-in preset, grouped by the capability area it serves: ```bash python -m cli connectors catalog # all presets python -m cli connectors catalog --area strategy-alignment python -m cli connectors catalog --json ``` | Capability area (`--area`) | Presets | |---|---| | Voice of customer & qualitative research (`voice-of-customer`) | `notion`, `gong`, `fireflies`, `intercom`, `confluence` | | Quantitative data & opportunity scoring (`quantitative-data`) | `posthog`, `amplitude`, `mixpanel` | | Market & competitive intelligence (`market-intelligence`) | `exa`, `tavily` | | Product strategy & backlog alignment (`strategy-alignment`) | `linear`, `github`, `jira`, `miro`, `figma` | | Strategy & knowledge management output (`knowledge-output`) | `slack` | Register one with `--preset`; `--name` defaults to the preset id: ```bash # Token-based preset: export the variable it needs first export GITHUB_PERSONAL_ACCESS_TOKEN=ghp_... python -m cli connectors add mcp --preset github python -m cli connectors health --name github python -m cli connectors ingest --name github # OAuth-based preset: the browser consent flow starts on first use python -m cli connectors add mcp --preset notion ``` Credentials never enter the registry. Presets that use API keys store `${VAR}` placeholders that are resolved from the environment when a connection is opened, and `connectors health` names any variable that is missing. `--url` overrides the endpoint (self-hosted or proxied deployments) and `--tool` still selects which tools to call during ingest. Custom servers keep working the same way: ```bash python -m cli connectors add mcp --name internal --url https://mcp.internal.example/mcp --tool latest_quote python -m cli connectors list ``` Ingested records are normalized (`catalog`, `resource`, `tool_result`) and appended to the in-process ingest sink. They are not written into the ODI jobs/outcomes store. > [!NOTE] > Presets cover MCP servers with a hosted endpoint. Servers you run yourself (Snowflake, BigQuery, Google Drive, Brave Search, and similar) are added with an explicit `--url`. The catalog lives in `connectors/src/connectors/catalog.py`. > [!NOTE] > OAuth tokens are cached in memory for the life of one CLI process, so an OAuth preset may ask for consent again on the next `connectors health` or `connectors ingest`. Prefer a token-based preset where the server offers one. ### ⚡ Living Studio Run Modes The Living Studio runs three ways. All of them serve the same SPA, which talks only to the sidecar on `http://127.0.0.1:8100` — the SPA never contacts MCP or the LLM directly. **Architecture** ```text ┌────────────────────────────┐ /api (JSON) ┌───────────────────────────────┐ │ Living Studio SPA │ ────────────▶ │ local_server (sidecar) │ │ React + TS + Vite │ /api/chat │ FastAPI on 127.0.0.1:8100 │ │ (browser or Tauri webview)│ ◀──────────── │ - config / health / canvas │ └────────────────────────────┘ SSE stream │ - steps / outcomes (via MCP) │ │ - /api/chat (LLM tool-loop) │ └───────────────┬───────────────┘ │ MCP (HTTP) ▼ ┌───────────────────────────────┐ │ mcp_server :8000/mcp │ └───────────────────────────────┘ ▲ │ OpenAI-compatible ┌───────────────┴───────────────┐ │ Your local LLM backend │ └───────────────────────────────┘ ``` **1. Web — production build (recommended for a quick look)** ```bash npm --prefix studio run build # build the SPA into studio/dist python -m client.run # starts MCP :8000 + sidecar :8100 ``` | Service | URL | |---|---| | MCP Server | http://localhost:8000/mcp | | Living Studio | http://127.0.0.1:8100 | **2. Web — dev with hot reload** (Vite proxies `/api` to the sidecar): ```bash npm --prefix studio run dev:full # MCP + sidecar + Vite together # open http://localhost:5173 ``` **3. Desktop — Tauri 2** (the app spawns the MCP server and sidecar itself): ```bash npm --prefix studio run tauri dev # dev window npm --prefix studio run tauri build # bundles: .deb / .AppImage (Linux), .app / .dmg (macOS), .msi / .exe (Windows) ``` > [!NOTE] > **Tauri prerequisites.** The desktop build needs the WebKitGTK toolchain and Rust 1.90+. On Debian/Ubuntu: > > ```bash > sudo apt-get install -y libwebkit2gtk-4.1-dev build-essential pkg-config curl wget file \ > libxdo-dev libssl-dev libayatana-appindicator3-dev librsvg2-dev patchelf xdg-utils libfuse2t64 > ``` > > The Tauri CLI ships as the `@tauri-apps/cli` npm dev dependency (`npm --prefix studio run tauri`). The sidecar is launched with `uv run python -m …` from the repository root; if the app cannot locate the repo root, set `AGENTIC_ODI_REPO_ROOT`. #### 🔐 Desktop signing & updater secrets Self-updating and code signing are **env-driven**: if a secret is absent, an unsigned artifact is produced instead of failing. CI reads these from GitHub Actions secrets. | Secret | Purpose | |---|---| | `TAURI_SIGNING_PRIVATE_KEY` | Signs updater artifacts (`.sig`) and the `latest.json` manifest. A tagged release fails loudly without it. Generate with `npm --prefix studio run tauri signer generate`. | | `TAURI_SIGNING_PRIVATE_KEY_PASSWORD` | Password for the private key (optional when the key has none). | | `APPLE_CERTIFICATE` / `APPLE_CERTIFICATE_PASSWORD` | macOS Developer ID certificate (base64 `.p12`) and its password. | | `APPLE_SIGNING_IDENTITY` | macOS signing identity. | | `APPLE_ID` / `APPLE_PASSWORD` / `APPLE_TEAM_ID` | macOS notarization credentials. | | `WINDOWS_CERTIFICATE` / `WINDOWS_CERTIFICATE_PASSWORD` | Windows Authenticode PFX (base64) and its password; imported by CI and injected into the bundle config. | Releases are published by `.github/workflows/tauri-release.yml` when a `v*` tag is pushed. The desktop app checks for updates on startup and via **Settings → Check for updates**. #### 🔑 Managing the updater signing key The updater key pair authenticates release artifacts so an installed app can verify that an auto-update genuinely came from you. The **public** key is embedded in `studio/src-tauri/tauri.conf.json` (`plugins.updater.pubkey`) and is safe to commit. The **private** key must never be committed, logged, printed in CI, or attached to a build artifact. 1. **Generate a key pair** (only if you need a new one). Leave `-p ""` for a passwordless key, or pass a password and remember it: ```bash npm --prefix studio run tauri signer generate -- -w ./living-studio.key -p "" -f ``` This writes `living-studio.key` (private, `0600`) and `living-studio.key.pub` (public). 2. **Paste the public key** into `studio/src-tauri/tauri.conf.json`: ```jsonc { "plugins": { "updater": { "endpoints": ["https://github.com/alehar9320/agentic-odi/releases/latest/download/latest.json"], "pubkey": "" } } } ``` 3. **Store the private key outside the repository** (the repo root is git-tracked; a sibling directory is not), with restricted permissions: ```bash mkdir -p ~/repos/agentic-odi-keys && chmod 700 ~/repos/agentic-odi-keys mv living-studio.key ~/repos/agentic-odi-keys/ chmod 600 ~/repos/agentic-odi-keys/living-studio.key ``` Move it to a long-term secret store (password manager, 1Password/Bitwarden/Vault, or a private encrypted backup) when you decide where that lives. Losing it means future releases can no longer be signed for existing installs. 4. **Add the private key as a GitHub Actions secret** (Settings → Secrets and variables → Actions → New repository secret), or via the CLI: ```bash gh secret set TAURI_SIGNING_PRIVATE_KEY < ~/repos/agentic-odi-keys/living-studio.key gh secret set TAURI_SIGNING_PRIVATE_KEY_PASSWORD --body "" # only if you set a password ``` 5. **Verify** the secrets exist (values are never displayed): ```bash gh secret list ``` 6. **Rotate** by repeating steps 1–4, then publishing a release signed with the new key. Existing installs still verify against the public key compiled into their binary, so keep the old private key usable and publish the new public key ahead of the cut-over. > [!CAUTION] > If the private key leaks, treat auto-updates as compromised: generate a new pair, rotate the Actions secret, and publish a freshly signed release. > [!IMPORTANT] > **Migration note.** The Streamlit UI (`client/src/client/app.py`) has been removed. The Living Studio now lives in `studio/` (browser SPA + Tauri desktop app) and is served by the `local_server` sidecar on port **8100** (previously Streamlit's `8501`). Start everything with `python -m client.run`. All `AGENTIC_ODI_*` environment variable names, the demo dataset, and the ODI formulas are unchanged. ### 🧠 Local Tools-Capable LLM Backend (for MCP testing) To exercise real tool-calling end-to-end against the MCP server, you need a local LLM backend that: - Exposes an **OpenAI-compatible Chat Completions API** (for example, `/v1/chat/completions`), and - Supports OpenAI-style **`tools` / `tool_calls`**. A simple fully local option is [`llama-cpp-python`](https://github.com/abetlen/llama-cpp-python), which can run a quantized model on your machine and expose an OpenAI-compatible server. 1. **Install a local LLM server** Install `llama-cpp-python` in your environment (see its README for platform-specific build notes): ```bash pip install llama-cpp-python ``` 2. **Download a small tools-capable model** Download a small GGUF model that supports function/tool calling (for example, a 7B function-calling variant from Hugging Face) and note its path, e.g. `C:\models\local-tools-model.gguf`. 3. **Start the OpenAI-compatible server** Start the server and give the model a friendly alias that matches the default used by the Living Studio sidecar: ```bash python -m llama_cpp.server \ --model "C:\models\local-tools-model.gguf" \ --model_alias local-tools-model \ --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8001 \ --chat_format openai ``` This exposes an OpenAI-style API at `http://127.0.0.1:8001/v1`. 4. **Point the Living Studio at the local server** The sidecar reads defaults from environment variables (with sensible fallbacks): | Variable | Default | |---|---| | `AGENTIC_ODI_BASE_URL` | `http://localhost:8001/v1` | | `AGENTIC_ODI_MODEL` | `local-tools-model` | | `AGENTIC_ODI_MCP_URL` | `http://localhost:8000/mcp` | | `AGENTIC_ODI_API_KEY` | `local` | You can either set these in your shell or adjust them in the Living Studio's **Settings** panel. 5. **Verify tool-calling against the MCP server** - (Optional) Before starting the UI, confirm the LLM backend is reachable: ```bash curl http://127.0.0.1:8001/v1/models ``` If this request fails, fix your local LLM server configuration before debugging the MCP client/server. - Start the MCP server and the Living Studio (via `python -m client.run` or `npm --prefix studio run dev:full`). - In the browser UI, ask the assistant something that should use ODI tools, for example: “Help me define a new Job-to-be-Done and add it to your ODI repository.” - You should see the assistant briefly display that it is calling tools (for example, `add_job`, `get_jobs`, etc.) and then respond with grounded ODI guidance, confirming that the local LLM, MCP server, and client wiring all work together. - If the LLM backend is unreachable or misconfigured, the UI will show a clear error banner indicating that the backend at your configured **Base URL** could not be reached, along with details from the underlying error. Use that message together with the steps above to fix your local LLM setup. ### 🤖 Agent-Driven Testing Type `/dev` in the AI assistant to trigger the full automated workflow: it will start both processes, open the browser, send a test message, and report the results. --- ## 🧹 Linting, Formatting & Type Checks (CI parity) The CI pipeline runs several quality checks. Install the latest release with one command: ```bash curl -fsSL https://github.com/alehar9320/agentic-odi/releases/latest/download/install.sh | sh ``` The installer places the binary under `~/.local/share/agentic-odi/versions//`, creates a `current` symlink, and symlinks `odi`, `odipm`, `odi-cli`, and `agentic-odi` into `~/.local/bin/`. If `~/.local/bin` is not on your PATH, add it (e.g., `export PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH"`). On Windows, the PowerShell installer uses `~\AppData\Local\agentic-odi\` and copies `.exe` files to `~\AppData\Local\agentic-odi\bin\`. ### Update By default, `odi` auto-checks for updates once every 24 hours and applies the update on the next run (auto-update is enabled by default). Control behavior with: - `odi update` — explicit check and update - `--no-update` flag — skip auto-update for this run - `AGENTIC_ODI_NO_UPDATE=1` — disable auto-update globally When running from a non-frozen source install, auto-update is suppressed automatically. ### Install layout ``` ~/.local/share/agentic-odi/ ├── versions// │ └── odi (and bundled files) └── current -> versions/ ~/.local/bin/ ├── odi -> ../share/agentic-odi/current/odi ├── odipm ├── odi-cli └── agentic-odi ~/.config/agentic-odi/ # state/preferences ``` Environment variables: `AGENTIC_ODI_INSTALL_DIR` (override install root), `XDG_DATA_HOME`, `XDG_BIN_HOME`. The default backend is `local` (`--backend local`); no MCP server is required. ### Unsigned binaries macOS may quarantine downloaded binaries: `xattr -d com.apple.quarantine ~/.local/bin/odi` (if needed). Windows SmartScreen may show a warning for unsigned binaries; choose "More info → Run anyway" if you trust the release. ### Release automation Releases are cut and published by CI with no approval step: 1. Conventional commits land on `main`; `release-please` opens or updates the release PR. 2. The `release-please` workflow arms auto-merge on that PR. `main` requires the `CI green` check (ruleset `main-requires-ci-green`), so the PR merges itself as soon as CI passes — nobody clicks merge. 3. The merge cuts tag `vX.Y.Z` and the GitHub Release; the tag starts the `release` and `Tauri Release` workflows, which attach the CLI archives, `checksums.txt`, the install scripts, and the desktop bundles to it. 4. `e2e-install` runs after `release` succeeds and installs the published binary on Linux, macOS, and Windows. **One-time setup (GitHub App).** GitHub holds workflow runs that start from `GITHUB_TOKEN`-authored pushes ("This workflow requires approval from a maintainer") and ignores the tag such a push creates, which is why releases used to need a maintainer. A release-only GitHub App avoids both: 1. Settings → Developer settings → GitHub Apps → New GitHub App, with permissions: Contents `Read and write`, Issues `Read and write`, Pull requests `Read and write` (no webhook). 2. Install the App on this repository. 3. Add repository secrets `RELEASE_PLEASE_APP_CLIENT_ID` (the App's client ID) and `RELEASE_PLEASE_APP_PRIVATE_KEY` (a generated private key). +# Living Studio: Intent-First Product Management
+
+The Living Studio is an interactive, conversational environment for product managers to focus on their career-defining opportunities. It leverages Model Context Protocol (MCP) to connect the product manager's intent with outcome-driven innovation.
+
+## The Vision
+
+The Living Studio has been redesigned to focus on **product managers' ambition** rather than ODI methodology. The agent now interprets PMs' career-defining opportunities and helps them win them, rather than explaining frameworks.
+
+**North Star:** Help me choose and win the next opportunity that matters — to customers, the business, and my career.
+
+## Key Features
+
+1. **Intent-First Agent**: The system prompt has been rewritten to prioritize PM ambition and silent translation of ODI concepts into actionable outcomes. The agent now proposes observations and asks for confirmation, creating a "living memory" of the conversation.
+
+2. **Local Studio Memory**: A SQLite-backed store persists conversations and observations (`career`, `opportunity`, `business`, etc.) across sessions. The "What I've learned" panel shows these observations and allows the PM to confirm, edit, or dismiss them.
+
+3. **Opportunity Thesis**: The default canvas focus is the **Opportunity Thesis** card, which presents one opportunity with its importance, current state, and the gap to be closed. This replaces the traditional Opportunity Landscape.
+
+4. **Ambition-Driven Onboarding**: The first-run wizard now presents four doors based on the PM's intent:
+   - "I have an opportunity in mind"
+   - "My boss handed me a priority"
+   - "I need to find one"
+   - "Pressure-test an idea"
+
+5. **Session Persistence**: Conversations are persisted via the `conversationId` and `memory` SSE events, allowing the PM to resume from where they left off.
+
+6. **Explainability**: The agent uses a `remember` tool to propose observations, which are stored in the local memory store and displayed in the MemoryPanel.
+
+## How to Use
+
+1. **Start the Living Studio**:
+   ```bash
+   python -m client.run
+   ```
+   This launches the MCP server and the Studio sidecar.
+
+2. **Access the Studio**:
+   Open your browser at `http://127.0.0.1:8100`.
+
+3. **Interact**:
+   - The agent will greet you and ask about your intent.
+   - Use the chat interface to discuss your opportunity.
+   - The agent will propose observations and ask for confirmation.
+   - Review the "What I've learned" panel to see your conversation history.
+
+4. **Persist Your Work**:
+   The Studio automatically saves your conversation and observations. They will be available the next time you start the application.
+
+## Technical Details
+
+- **Backend**: FastAPI with FastMCP integration.
+- **Database**: SQLite (local storage at `~/.agentic-odi/studio.db`).
+- **Frontend**: React with TypeScript and Vite.
+- **Agent**: Local tools-capable LLM backend (e.g., llama-cpp-python) with OpenAI-compatible API.
+
+## Contributing
+
+If you'd like to contribute to the Living Studio, please refer to the main repository's contributing guidelines.

| "This doesn't need a formal skill" | If a skill exists, use it. |
| "I remember this skill" | Skills evolve. Read current version. |
| "This doesn't count as a task" | Action = task. Check for skills. |
| "The skill is overkill" | Simple things become complex. Use it. |
| "I'll just do this one thing first" | Check BEFORE doing anything. |
| "This feels productive" | Undisciplined action wastes time. Skills prevent it. |
| "I know what that means" | Knowing the concept ≠ using the skill. Invoke it. |

## Platform Adaptation

If your harness appears here, read its reference file for special instructions:

- Kiro: `.agents/skills/using-superpowers/references/kiro-tools.md`
- Freebuff: `.agents/skills/using-superpowers/references/freebuff-tools.md`
- Claude Code: `.agents/skills/using-superpowers/references/claude-code-tools.md`
- Codex: `.agents/skills/using-superpowers/references/codex-tools.md`
- Pi: `.agents/skills/using-superpowers/references/pi-tools.md`
- Antigravity: `.agents/skills/using-superpowers/references/antigravity-tools.md`
- Hermes Agent: `.agents/skills/using-superpowers/references/hermes-tools.md`
- Muse: `.agents/skills/using-superpowers/references/muse-tools.md`

## User Instructions

User instructions (CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md, GEMINI.md, etc, direct requests) take precedence over skills, which in turn override default behavior. Only skip skill workflows or instructions when your human partner has explicitly told you to.

## Kiro Tool Mapping

Skills speak in actions, not tool names. On Kiro CLI they resolve as follows:

| Action skills request | Kiro CLI equivalent |
| --- | --- |
| Invoke or load a skill | Read the skill's `SKILL.md` with the `read` tool and follow its instructions directly |
| Create a todo / mark one complete | `todo_list` (create, add, complete, remove commands) |
| Read a file | `read` tool (Line or Directory mode) |
| Create or overwrite a file | `write` tool (create command) |
| Edit a file in place | `write` tool (strReplace command) |
| Delete, move, or rename a file | `shell` tool (`rm`, `mv`) |
| Run a shell command | `shell` tool |
| Search file contents | `grep` tool (regex pattern search) |
| Search by symbol / semantic code search | `code` tool (search_symbols, pattern_search, etc.) |
| Find files by name | `glob` tool |
| List a directory | `read` tool (Directory mode) |
| Fetch a URL | `web_fetch` tool |
| Search the web | `web_search` tool |
| Ask your human partner a question | Respond to the user in your message |
| Dispatch a subagent (`Subagent (general-purpose):` template) | `subagent` tool with a `kiro_default` stage (blocking mode) |
| Enter plan mode | `todo_list` to track steps; write designs to `docs/superpowers/specs/YYYY-MM-DD-<topic>-design.md` |
| Persist progress across compaction | Write the ledger and briefs under `.superpowers/sdd/<plan-basename>/` (see `executing-plans`) |

Skills live in `.agents/skills/*/SKILL.md`. Kiro has no automatic skill-loading tool — read a `SKILL.md` with the `read` tool before following it.

For the full Kiro tool reference including subagent dispatch patterns and git worktree instructions, read `.agents/skills/using-superpowers/references/kiro-tools.md`.

- Run `uv run pytest` from the root; see `.agents/workflows/test.md` and `docs/architecture/testing.md` for focused commands.

# CI-green sweep over the open PRs — plan

> **For agentic workers:** REQUIRED SUB-SKILL: Use superpowers:executing-plans to implement this plan task-by-task. Steps use checkbox (`- [ ]`) syntax for tracking.

**Goal:** Every open PR on `alehar9320/agentic-odi` reports the `CI green` required check, so nothing is stuck behind a merge conflict.

**Architecture:** The required check is `CI green` (ruleset `main-requires-ci-green`), which aggregates lint, typecheck, security, test (3.10/3.11/3.12), smoke, studio, tauri-check and tauri-build. GitHub never runs CI on a conflicting PR, so the actual work is: rebase each PR branch onto `main`, resolve the conflicts, fix whatever the merge broke, push, and wait for the check. Work happens in one git worktree per PR under `.worktrees/`.

**Tech Stack:** git worktrees, `uv` (ruff/mypy/bandit/pytest), npm (eslint/tsc/vitest/vite), cargo (fmt/clippy), GitHub CLI, Jules (as a delegated implementer).

**Spec:** This plan. The sweep is a maintenance task, not a feature.

## Global Constraints

- Base every rebase on the then-current `origin/main`; re-`git fetch origin` before each one.
- Rebase the single commit on each branch and `git push --force-with-lease` to the same branch. Never merge a PR by hand.
- One worktree per PR under `.worktrees/` (already excluded via `.git/info/exclude`). Do not touch the root working tree: its `main` is 52 commits behind and its untracked `apps/` is stale leftover.
- The local gate mirrors CI: `uv run ruff check .` + `uv run ruff format --check .`; `uv run mypy apps packages` + `uv run --directory website mypy .`; `uv run bandit -c pyproject.toml -r apps packages` + website; `uv run pytest` (root, then on 3.10/3.11/3.12); `uv run --directory website pytest tests/`; in `apps/studio`: `npm ci && npm run lint && npm run typecheck && npm test -- --run && npm run build && npm run gen:api-types` with `git diff --exit-code -- src/api/schema.d.ts`; smoke (CLI version, connectors help, `scripts/tests/install_e2e.sh`, MCP server boot, sidecar boot, `scripts/dev.py` boot); `cargo fmt --check && cargo clippy -- -D warnings && cargo check`.
- Run `pytest` **before** `npm run build` in a worktree: a built `apps/studio/dist` makes the sidecar serve the SPA and turns unknown routes into 200s, which breaks `test_unknown_route_is_404`. CI never sees this because its jobs are separate checkouts.
- `apps/studio/openapi.json` is hand-kept and `src/api/schema.d.ts` is generated from it. When a PR changes the sidecar API surface, regenerate both: `uv run python -c "import json; from agentic_odi_studio_api.app import create_app; open('apps/studio/openapi.json','w').write(json.dumps(create_app().openapi(), indent=2) + '\n')"` then `npm run gen:api-types`.
- Keep `README.md` and `docs/` in the same commit as any user-visible change.

## Review Focus

- A conflict resolved by dropping one side silently loses a feature. Every conflict resolution must keep main's newer behaviour *and* the PR's contribution.
- Auto-merged files can still be semantically broken (a new required field missing from a literal, an import dropped). The type checker and the test suite are what catch this — run them, don't trust the merge.
- Deleting a test file to make a suite pass is not a resolution. Keep main's coverage and add the PR's.
- The `CI green` job is the only required check, but `Workers Builds` (Cloudflare) is a separate external check owned by another agent working on the Cloudflare build.

## The Rule

**Invoke relevant or requested skills BEFORE any response or action** — including clarifying questions, exploring the codebase, or checking files. If it turns out wrong for the situation, you don't have to use it.

**Before entering plan mode:** if you haven't already brainstormed, invoke the brainstorming skill first.

## Skill Priority

When multiple skills apply, process skills come first — they set the approach, then implementation skills (frontend-design, etc.) carry it out. Brainstorming and systematic-debugging are Superpowers' most common process skills, but the rule holds for any of them.

- "Let's build X" → superpowers:brainstorming first, then implementation skills.
- "Fix this bug" → superpowers:systematic-debugging first, then domain skills.

## Red Flags

These thoughts mean STOP—you're rationalizing:

| Thought | Reality |
|---------|---------|
| "This is just a simple question" | Questions are tasks. Check for skills. |
| "I need more context first" | Skill check comes BEFORE clarifying questions. |
| "Let me explore the codebase first" | Skills tell you HOW to explore. Check first. |
| "I can check git/files quickly" | Files lack conversation context. Check for skills. |
| "Let me gather information first" | Skills tell you HOW to gather information. |

"""On-Device Fallback & Model Router module.

Provides multi-tier routing (Rule-based, On-Device Local LLM, Remote Smart LLM)
with automatic fallback and user settings support.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import asyncio
from collections.abc import AsyncIterator, Callable
from enum import Enum

from agentic_odi_core.steve_jobs import generate_steve_jobs_response


class ModelTier(str, Enum):
    """Model execution tiers."""

    RULE_BASED = "rule_based"  # Tier 0: On-device instant rule-based engine (Steve Jobs pass)
    ON_DEVICE_LLM = "on_device_llm"  # Tier 1: On-device / local GGUF / tiny model engine
    REMOTE_LLM = "remote_llm"  # Tier 2: Remote / smart cloud LLM backend


class RoutingMode(str, Enum):
    """Routing modes for model selection."""

    AUTO = "auto"  # Auto-select smartest available tier, transparent fallback
    FORCE_RULE_BASED = "rule_based"  # Force Tier 0
    FORCE_ON_DEVICE = "on_device"  # Force Tier 1
    FORCE_REMOTE = "remote"  # Force Tier 2


class OnDeviceLLMEngine:
    """Minimal lightweight on-device LLM engine wrapper / mock interface."""

    def __init__(self, model_name: str = "on-device-tiny-llm") -> None:
        self.model_name = model_name

    def is_available(self) -> bool:
        """Check if on-device model files/runtime are ready."""
        return True

    async def generate_stream(self, prompt: str) -> AsyncIterator[str]:
        """Generate response chunks from on-device model."""
        response = generate_steve_jobs_response(prompt)
        words = response.split(" ")
        for i, word in enumerate(words):
            chunk = word if i == 0 else " " + word
            yield chunk
            await asyncio.sleep(0.01)


class ModelRouter:
    """Intelligent router managing multi-tier execution and seamless fallback."""

    def __init__(
        self,
        mode: RoutingMode = RoutingMode.AUTO,
        on_device_engine: OnDeviceLLMEngine | None = None,
        remote_health_checker: Callable[[], tuple[bool, str]] | None = None,
    ) -> None:
        self.mode = mode
        self.on_device_engine = on_device_engine or OnDeviceLLMEngine()
        self.remote_health_checker = remote_health_checker

    def resolve_tier(self, remote_available: bool = False) -> ModelTier:
        """Resolve the appropriate tier based on routing mode and availability."""
        if self.mode == RoutingMode.FORCE_RULE_BASED:
            return ModelTier.RULE_BASED
        if self.mode == RoutingMode.FORCE_ON_DEVICE:
            return ModelTier.ON_DEVICE_LLM
        if self.mode == RoutingMode.FORCE_REMOTE:
            return ModelTier.REMOTE_LLM

        # AUTO mode logic
        if remote_available:
            return ModelTier.REMOTE_LLM
        if self.on_device_engine.is_available():
            return ModelTier.ON_DEVICE_LLM
        return ModelTier.RULE_BASED

    async def generate_fallback_stream(self, prompt: str, tier: ModelTier) -> AsyncIterator[str]:
        """Stream response for rule-based or on-device fallback tiers."""
        if tier == ModelTier.ON_DEVICE_LLM:
            async for chunk in self.on_device_engine.generate_stream(prompt):
                yield chunk
        else:

"""On-Device Fallback & Model Router module.

Provides multi-tier routing (Rule-based, On-Device Local LLM, Remote Smart LLM)
with automatic fallback and user settings support.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import asyncio
from collections.abc import AsyncIterator, Callable
from enum import Enum

from agentic_odi_core.steve_jobs import generate_steve_jobs_response


class ModelTier(str, Enum):
    """Model execution tiers."""

    RULE_BASED = "rule_based"  # Tier 0: On-device instant rule-based engine (Steve Jobs pass)
    ON_DEVICE_LLM = "on_device_llm"  # Tier 1: On-device / local GGUF / tiny model engine
    REMOTE_LLM = "remote_llm"  # Tier 2: Remote / smart cloud LLM backend


class RoutingMode(str, Enum):
    """Routing modes for model selection."""

    AUTO = "auto"  # Auto-select smartest available tier, transparent fallback
    FORCE_RULE_BASED = "rule_based"  # Force Tier 0
    FORCE_ON_DEVICE = "on_device"  # Force Tier 1
    FORCE_REMOTE = "remote"  # Force Tier 2


class OnDeviceLLMEngine:
    """Minimal lightweight on-device LLM engine wrapper / mock interface."""

    def __init__(self, model_name: str = "on-device-tiny-llm") -> None:
        self.model_name = model_name

    def is_available(self) -> bool:
        """Check if on-device model files/runtime are ready."""
        return True

    async def generate_stream(self, prompt: str) -> AsyncIterator[str]:
        """Generate response chunks from on-device model."""
        response = generate_steve_jobs_response(prompt)
        words = response.split(" ")
        for i, word in enumerate(words):
            chunk = word if i == 0 else " " + word
            yield chunk
            await asyncio.sleep(0.01)


class ModelRouter:
    """Intelligent router managing multi-tier execution and seamless fallback."""

    def __init__(
        self,
        mode: RoutingMode = RoutingMode.AUTO,
        on_device_engine: OnDeviceLLMEngine | None = None,
        remote_health_checker: Callable[[], tuple[bool, str]] | None = None,
    ) -> None:
        self.mode = mode
        self.on_device_engine = on_device_engine or OnDeviceLLMEngine()
        self.remote_health_checker = remote_health_checker

    def resolve_tier(self, remote_available: bool = False) -> ModelTier:
        """Resolve the appropriate tier based on routing mode and availability."""
        if self.mode == RoutingMode.FORCE_RULE_BASED:
            return ModelTier.RULE_BASED
        if self.mode == RoutingMode.FORCE_ON_DEVICE:
            return ModelTier.ON_DEVICE_LLM
        if self.mode == RoutingMode.FORCE_REMOTE:
            return ModelTier.REMOTE_LLM

        # AUTO mode logic
        if remote_available:
            return ModelTier.REMOTE_LLM
        if self.on_device_engine.is_available():
            return ModelTier.ON_DEVICE_LLM
        return ModelTier.RULE_BASED

    async def generate_fallback_stream(self, prompt: str, tier: ModelTier) -> AsyncIterator[str]:
        """Stream response for rule-based or on-device fallback tiers."""
        if tier == ModelTier.ON_DEVICE_LLM:
            async for chunk in self.on_device_engine.generate_stream(prompt):
                yield chunk
        else:
            # Rule-based Tier 0
            text = generate_steve_jobs_response(prompt)
            words = text.split(" ")
            for i, word in enumerate(words):
                chunk = word if i == 0 else " " + word
                yield chunk
                await asyncio.sleep(0.005)

async def stream_chat(
    request: ChatRequest, service: ConnectorService | None = None
) -> AsyncIterator[str]:
    """Yield SSE frames: status, delta, tool, ui, connector, message, canvas_dirty."""
    yield _sse("status", {"phase": "health_check"})
    healthy, _message = await check_llm_health(request.base_url, request.api_key, request.model)

    last_user = next((m.content for m in reversed(request.messages) if m.role == "user"), "")

    if not healthy:
        yield _sse("status", {"phase": "offline"})
        reply = offline_fallback(last_user, request.brief)
        yield _sse("delta", {"text": reply})
        yield _sse("message", {"content": reply})
        return

    catalog = UiCatalog.from_manifest(
        request.ui_catalog.model_dump() if request.ui_catalog else None
    )

    yield _sse("status", {"phase": "mcp_tools"})
    llm_client = AsyncOpenAI(base_url=request.base_url, api_key=request.api_key, timeout=15.0)

# Local Tools-Capable LLM Backend

To exercise real tool-calling end-to-end against the MCP server, you need a
local LLM backend that:

- Exposes an **OpenAI-compatible Chat Completions API** (for example,
  `/v1/chat/completions`), and
- Supports OpenAI-style **`tools` / `tool_calls`**.

A simple fully local option is
[`llama-cpp-python`](https://github.com/abetlen/llama-cpp-python), which can run
a quantized model on your machine and expose an OpenAI-compatible server.

## 1. Install a local LLM server

Install `llama-cpp-python` in your environment (see its README for
platform-specific build notes):

```bash
pip install llama-cpp-python
```

## 2. Download a small tools-capable model

Download a small GGUF model that supports function/tool calling (for example, a
7B function-calling variant from Hugging Face) and note its path, e.g.
`C:\models\local-tools-model.gguf`.

## 3. Start the OpenAI-compatible server

Start the server and give the model a friendly alias that matches the default
used by the Living Studio sidecar and the CLI chat:

```bash
python -m llama_cpp.server \
  --model "C:\models\local-tools-model.gguf" \
  --model_alias local-tools-model \
  --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8001 \
  --chat_format openai
```

This exposes an OpenAI-style API at `http://127.0.0.1:8001/v1`.

## 4. Configure the Studio

The Living Studio sidecar and the CLI chat read the following environment
variables (with sensible defaults):

| Variable | Default |
|---|---|

metadata.output:
# Local Tools-Capable LLM Backend

To exercise real tool-calling end-to-end against the MCP server, you need a
local LLM backend that:

- Exposes an **OpenAI-compatible Chat Completions API** (for example,
  `/v1/chat/completions`), and
- Supports OpenAI-style **`tools` / `tool_calls`**.

A simple fully local option is
[`llama-cpp-python`](https://github.com/abetlen/llama-cpp-python), which can run
a quantized model on your machine and expose an OpenAI-compatible server.

## 1. Install a local LLM server

Install `llama-cpp-python` in your environment (see its README for
platform-specific build notes):

```bash
pip install llama-cpp-python
```

## 2. Download a small tools-capable model

Download a small GGUF model that supports function/tool calling (for example, a
7B function-calling variant from Hugging Face) and note its path, e.g.
`C:\models\local-tools-model.gguf`.

## 3. Start the OpenAI-compatible server

Start the server and give the model a friendly alias that matches the default
used by the Living Studio sidecar and the CLI chat:

```bash
python -m llama_cpp.server \
  --model "C:\models\local-tools-model.gguf" \
  --model_alias local-tools-model \
  --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8001 \
  --chat_format openai
```

This exposes an OpenAI-style API at `http://127.0.0.1:8001/v1`.

## 4. Configure the Studio

The Living Studio sidecar and the CLI chat read the following environment
variables (with sensible defaults):

| Variable | Default |
|---|---|
| `AGENTIC_ODI_BASE_URL` | `http://localhost:8001/v1` |
| `AGENTIC_ODI_MODEL` | `local-tools-model` |
| `AGENTIC_ODI_MCP_URL` | `http://localhost:8000/mcp` |
| `AGENTIC_ODI_API_KEY` | `local` |

You can either set these in your shell or adjust them in the Living Studio's
**Settings** panel.

## 5. Verify tool-calling against the MCP server


  banner indicating the configured **Base URL** could not be reached, along with
  details from the underlying error. Use that message together with the steps
  above to fix your local LLM setup.

**Merged during the sweep:** 67 (release 0.11.0), 71 (conversation-first), 73 (pages), 74 (Cloudflare previews), 75 (release 0.12.0).

## Notes you should know

- **Jules was only partly useful.** The `@jules` PR-comment route works and Jules pushed commits — but on 4 branches it only produced Cloudflare `wrangler.jsonc`/`package.json` edits, not the rebase I asked for. The `jules new` CLI is currently blocked account-wide (`FAILED_PRECONDITION`: 4 sessions still open, incl. the other agent's). I took those 4 PRs back and did them by hand.
- **I stripped the Cloudflare commits** Jules had pushed onto 62/63/65/66 — that work belongs to the other agent, and `main` already carries the `previews` block from #74. Those branches are clean of Cloudflare changes.
- **PR 66 is narrower than it was.** The `L0/L1/L2` engagement switcher and the collapsed-by-default settings panel were dropped, not ported: main removed the engagement-level concept, so re-adding that state is a new feature, not a mobile fix. The chat FAB/bottom-sheet were also dropped (chat is always on stage now). If you want any of those back, say which and I'll add them.
- **The release PR approval is a recurring tax.** `release-please` falls back to `GITHUB_TOKEN` (the `RELEASE_PLEASE_APP_*` secrets are missing), so every release PR's CI run waits for a maintainer. I approved PR 75's run via the API; PR 67's had already been approved and merged. Adding those two secrets would stop this.
